items.message: On a Friday in mid-July, a delivery truck arrived at the Mirelle Bay Pool Supply yard carrying a pallet of forty-eight jugs of liquid chlorinating solution. While being moved by forklift to the covered dock, the pallet fell and split open due to either broken paving or an uneven stack. Several jugs burst, and the liquid began spreading toward a yard drain. Warehouse staff acted quickly to place sand bags around the drain before emergency responders reached the scene. Tessin Fire Service logged the call and arrived shortly after, washing the remaining liquid into a temporary holding bund while firefighters wearing breathing apparatus moved the surviving jugs under a tarpaulin. A tanker operated by a licensed waste contractor collected the contained liquid the following morning. During the incident, the business park air monitor recorded chlorine levels rising above its alarm threshold, peaking before dropping back down later that afternoon. Yard cameras and gate logs successfully captured the full timeline of the delivery, the fall, and the immediate evacuation of workers to upwind areas.

An incident occurred at the Veltrane Dye Depot on the Orsel Canal wharf when a fire broke out in the cold-storage annex shortly after 04:00 on 22 October. The annex smoke detector panel recorded an alarm on zone 2 before any other zone reported, with the first alarm raised at 04:06. Security camera footage time-stamped 04:09 showed the annex roller door glowing orange at its lower edge. Cameras on the north wharf subsequently lost power at 04:31. The first emergency call was logged at 04:12 by a passing canal barge pilot who described flames visible through the annex upper vents, and the first pumper left the fire station at 04:14. Five appliances were at the scene at the peak of the response. Firefighters drew water from the Orsel Canal using a floating suction hose, and the wharf road was closed until mid-morning. One firefighter was treated for a minor wrist burn. 

Imre Dallow, the sole supervisor on site, led six warehouse staff out through the loading door, and a subsequent headcount accounted for everyone within minutes. Dallow had noted the refrigeration compressors running normally during a 03:30 walk-round. The annex contained about 40 pallets of powdered pigment and refrigerated dye concentrate. An insurance loss adjuster estimated that the annex roof collapsed entirely while the main warehouse suffered only smoke and water damage.

Harnsey Fish Works, Lantern Quay, Thornwick Sands: Incident Report, Cold Store 2 Gas Leak

At approximately 1:48 a.m. on a Thursday in July, the fixed detector panel in Cold Store 2 registered its first high-level alarm, and the suspected gas leak was logged with the Thornwick Sands Gas Board at 1:56 a.m. The Shift Log records 14 workers on shift in the plant when the alarm sounded. Night shift supervisor Odile Brandt heard the detector horn from the packing hall and ordered cold store staff out. She reported that no one presented symptoms to her at the muster point beside the ice plant. The detector's peak reading reached 38 percent of the lower explosive limit, and readings fell below the alarm threshold at 3:05 a.m.

A gas board engineer was assigned to the incoming propane supply line and reached the cold store doors before the fire brigade arrived on the quay. Tomas Verrill's brigade crew was the first to enter the store, wearing breathing apparatus, and the brigade later established a cordon extending about 60 meters from the doors. On Brandt's instruction, the packing hall extraction fans were switched off. The crew declared Cold Store 2 clear for re-entry after taking readings at its doorways. Frozen stock was moved to Cold Store 1 later that morning.

Two refrigerated trucks from Rennick Haulage were waiting at the loading dock when the alarm began. Both left the quay gate before 2:20 a.m. without their loads. The records differ on how long the loading dock remained closed: the Shift Log cites about two hours, while the Rennick Haulage Gate Ledger cites about four hours. This discrepancy should be reconciled before the report is finalized.

items.message: The incident at Kestrel Ridge Observatory began when the grid supply to the site dropped out at 00:58 and the standby generator started automatically about twenty seconds later. The generator ran for 38 minutes before it shut down at 01:36 while the grid remained out. The controller recorded a stop event followed by a lockout state requiring a manual reset at the generator panel. Sources disagree on the cause of the shutdown. The site engineer, Talwen Pryce, attributed the stop solely to overheating protection tripping after snow blocked the cooling air intake, while night operator Imre Soller attributed it solely to low oil pressure protection tripping. The fuel tank gauge record shows 61 percent at 01:00 and 48 percent at 02:00, with no sudden drop in level between 01:00 and 02:10, which suggests fuel supply was not the cause. The dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 because of incoming snow, and the access road was closed by snow that night, which limited outside assistance. Pryce walked the 300 metres from the staff cottage through the snow in about ten minutes, reset the lockout, and restarted the unit at 02:04. Accounts also differ on the order of the power loss. Soller reported that the control room lights went out and the dome drive fell silent while the battery-backed computers stayed on. Shift handover notes state that the control room lighting went out first and the dome drive lost power only afterward, while Soller's account describes the dome drive losing power first. The uninterruptible power supply carrying the telescope control computers was rated for about 25 minutes of runtime, which is shorter than the outage duration. The handover notes also record that the generator's last routine test run was 11 days before the storm. Visiting astronomer Dr. Odalys Renk was in the visitor wing preparing data and reported that corridor lights went dark when the generator noise faded.

items.message:
Varnholt Swing Bridge Closing Failure, Early March

On a Tuesday in early March, the Varnholt Swing Bridge was closed to all road and foot traffic after its rotating span came to rest about 14 centimetres short of full seating on the rest piers. The position encoder recorded the span stopping at 09:52, while the Operations Log records the stop at 10:04. The encoder record shows the span rotating to 90 degrees open and later returning to within a small margin of its closed angle without reaching the final seated value. Bridge operator Imre Valtonen, on duty in the control cabin, had started the opening sequence for the sailing barge Marl Heron. The 31-metre barge passed through the channel opening without contact with the fender piles. After the opening, a second closing attempt was made. The span moved less than one centimetre before the motor current limit tripped, and the encoder record confirms this movement. Valtonen reported that the closing motor ran at normal pitch but the end-of-travel light stayed unlit, and he telephoned the port engineer's on-call line after the second attempt. Both road barriers were lowered before the opening began and remained down after the failed seating. At the east barrier, seven vehicles were queued when the span came to rest, and a cyclist, Tobias Renwick, was waiting there on his bicycle. Pedestrians were permitted to walk back from the barrier along the eastern footway to the quay road. Harbourmaster Odile Brandvik ordered a vessel hold so that no further barges would be passed until the bridge was resolved, and the channel remained closed to vessels through the evening. Buses were held at the Varnholt Green stop while drivers were briefed, and the number 6 service was diverted by way of the Quillon Ring Road, adding roughly 20 minutes to the route.

On a Thursday in May, at 1:26 p.m., the freight elevator in the Finishing Building stopped between the second and third floors while travelling upward. Teodor Bram was in the car with a cart of fabric bolts. The controller recorded a safety-circuit stop command and a load of 1,140 kilograms; the unit’s rated capacity was 1,500 kilograms. Bram used the in-car call button and contacted the security desk through the intercom. The desk logged the call at 1:27 p.m.

Imogen Pask went to the third-floor landing and spoke with Bram through the closed outer doors. Dorrel Vance signed in at the gate at 1:48 p.m., went to the roof machine room, and isolated the elevator’s main power supply. He manually released the brake in short steps to lower the car to the second-floor landing. Accounts differ on the duration: Bram reported about 25 minutes, while the security desk log indicates about 40 minutes. Bram stepped out at the second floor unhurt. Pask moved the remaining fabric bolts to the third floor using the stairs and small passenger lift.

The work order identifies the elevator as a traction freight unit, notes its last scheduled inspection was in March, and records that it was tagged out of service until the following morning. The controller log shows the safety circuit reset after power was restored at 8:05 a.m. the next day. The stated causes conflict: the work order attributes the stop to the overspeed governor tripping on the upward run, while Vance attributes it to a worn third-floor door interlock contact.

The incident occurred at approximately 3:05 p.m. on a Friday in mid-July, when a pallet of chlorinating solution fell from a forklift in the loading yard of Mirelle Bay Pool Supply and split open. The generator controller recorded a stop event followed by a lockout state that required a manual reset at the generator panel. Two accounts conflict on the cause. The dome shutter had already been closed at 00:50 because of incoming snow. The uninterruptible power supply feeding the telescope control computers was rated for about 25 minutes of runtime. The site engineer walked from the staff cottage through the snow in about ten minutes and restarted the generator at 02:04 after resetting the lockout. Card payments at the pharmacy counter failed, so staff accepted only cash until the afternoon. Harbour Master Tobias Reld reported that the sea was calm overnight, with winds below 10 knots, and that no vessels were anchored near the cable route after dark.

Varnholt Swing Bridge closure, early March. On the day in question, the bridge was closed to all road and foot traffic after its rotating span stopped about 14 centimetres short of full seating on the rest piers. The encoder record shows the span came to rest at 09:52, while the Operations Log records the stop at 10:04; the discrepancy between these timestamps should be reconciled during review.

The operator on duty in the control cabin, Imre Valtonen, started the opening sequence for the sailing barge Marl Heron, a 31-metre vessel that passed through the channel opening without contact with the fender piles. Road barriers on both approaches were lowered before the opening began and remained down after the failed seating. Valtonen then made a second closing attempt. Both the Operations Log and the encoder record show the span moving less than one centimetre during that attempt before the motor current limit tripped and the span stopped. Valtonen reported that the closing motor ran at normal pitch but the end-of-travel light stayed unlit, and he telephoned the port engineer's on-call line after the second attempt.

Harbourmaster Odile Brandvik ordered a vessel hold so that no further barges would be passed until the bridge was resolved, and the channel remained closed to vessels through the evening. Seven vehicles were queued at the east barrier when the span came to rest. A cyclist waiting there was allowed to walk back along the eastern footway to the quay road. At the Varnholt Green stop, buses were held while drivers were briefed on the diversion; the number 6 service was routed by way of the Quillon Ring Road, adding roughly 20 minutes to its route.

Freight train 7114 derailed on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch at about 05:40 on a Tuesday in early March. It had left Kestrel Junction with two locomotives and 26 cars. The signal at the curve displayed a clear aspect. About six miles before the curve, the train passed the Milepost 41 detector at 38 miles per hour; the detector registered no overheated axle bearings.

Engineer Dalia Ronk felt a sudden lurch through the cab floor and applied the emergency brake. Shortly after the emergency brake alert, dispatcher Imre Voss received the call and halted all traffic on the branch. Seven cars left the rails, three overturning on the embankment. Bundles of timber from two overturned cars slid toward the river’s edge, and fertilizer bags split open on the slope.

Two crew members rode in the lead locomotive; both walked away without needing transport. The ambulance crew arrived 19 minutes after the call and treated Ronk at the scene for a bruised shoulder.

Recovery required two heavy cranes to lift the overturned cars. Crews replaced about 90 meters of track after clearing the cars. Spilled fertilizer was shoveled into containers. The line reopened at 14:10 on Thursday, though another report states it reopened at 21:30 that day; the discrepancy requires reconciliation.
